Cylinders and the zero locus of the plinth idealThanks: The study was implemented in the framework of the Basic Research Program at HSE University (HSE-BR-2025-84).

Kirill Shakhmatov Address: HSE University, Faculty of Computer Science, Pokrovsky Boulevard 11, Moscow, 109028 Russia Email address: kshahmatov@hse.ru
Abstract.

Given a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on an affine variety XX, we show that the complement of the union of all principal invariant cylinders in XX is equal to the zero locus of the plinth ideal of the corresponding locally nilpotent derivation.

Key words and phrases:
Affine variety, cylinder, locally nilpotent derivation, plinth ideal
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14R10, 14R20; Secondary 13A50

1. Introduction

We fix an algebraically closed field 𝕂\mathbb{K} of characteristic zero. By a variety we mean an integral separated scheme of finite type over 𝕂\mathbb{K}. Denote by 𝔾a=(𝕂,+)\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}=(\mathbb{K},+) the one-dimensional unipotent algebraic group.

The study of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions on algebraic varieties is a long-standing subject in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra. In addition to the fact that a description of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions is an object of study in itself, the algebraic nature of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions on affine varieties provides a technique that allows to tackle various problems. One example is the study of automorphism groups [8], [4]. Another is the Zariski Cancellation Problem. Exponential maps – a description of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions in the case of positive characteristic – were used by Gupta in [5] to provide counterexamples to the Zariski Cancellation problem in positive characteristic.

The results of the papers [6] and [7] provide a way to describe 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions using cylinders, that is, open subsets of the form 𝔸1×Z\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z. In particular, this technique can be used to study 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions on affine cones over a projective variety XX in terms of internal geometric properties of XX. This method was used in [1] to solve a long-standing problem about absence of non-trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions on affine Fermat cubic threefold.

Let XX be an affine variety. Then 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions on XX are in one-to-one correspondence with locally nilpotent derivations on the algebra 𝕂⁡[X]\mathbb{K}[X] of regular functions on XX. Given a locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial on a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra BB, the ideal pl(∂)=Ker∂∩Im∂\pl(\partial)=\Ker\partial\cap\mIm\partial in Ker∂\Ker\partial is called the plinth ideal of ∂\partial. Factorial affine varieties with 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions having principal plinth ideal were studied in [9]. In this note we obtain a geometric description of the zero locus 𝕍X​(pl⁡(∂))\mathbb{V}_{X}(\pl(\partial)) of the plinth ideal.

Let α:𝔾a×X→X\alpha\colon\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}\times X\to X be a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on an affine variety XX. By [6, Proposition 3.1.5] there exists a principal cylinder U≅𝔸1×ZU\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z in XX such that every 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fiber of UU is an orbit of α\alpha. We are interested in the geometric locus of the union of such cylinders. One can view this union as the locus of points in XX where the quotient X→YX\to Y, Y=Spec(Ker∂)Y=\Spec(\Ker\partial) admits a local principal trivialization of the action α\alpha.

This note consists of two sections. The main result of the first section is Theorem 2.6, in which it is proved that the union of principal cylinders defined by an action α\alpha coincides with the complement of the zero locus 𝕍X​(pl⁡(∂))\mathbb{V}_{X}(\pl(\partial)). In the second section we provide counterexamples to several natural assumptions, showing that this description does not admit a direct simplification.

The author is grateful to Ivan Arzhantsev and Sergey Gaifullin for useful discussions and suggestions.

2. Cylinders and the plinth ideal

Let us introduce basic definitions and conventions.

Let XX be a variety and S⊆𝕂⁡[X]S\subseteq\mathbb{K}[X] be a set of regular functions on XX. Denote by 𝕍X​(S)\mathbb{V}_{X}(S) the closed subvariety in XX given by equations h=0h=0 for h∈Sh\in S. Denote 𝔻X​(S)=X∖𝕍X​(S)\mathbb{D}_{X}(S)=X\setminus\mathbb{V}_{X}(S).

Let GG be an algebraic group and XX be a variety. By an action of GG on XX we mean a regular action G×X→XG\times X\to X. Consider an action α:G×X→X\alpha\colon G\times X\to X. We denote by Fix⁡(α)\Fix(\alpha) the set of fixed points of the action α\alpha. Given an invariant subvariety Y⊆XY\subseteq X, we denote by α|Y\left.\kern-1.2pt{\alpha}\right|_{Y} the induced action G×Y→YG\times Y\to Y.

Let BB be a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra. A locally nilpotent derivation (abbreviated LND) on BB is a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-derivation ∂:B→B\partial\colon B\to B satisfying the following property: for each b∈Bb\in B there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that ∂n(b)=0\partial^{n}(b)=0. The set of all locally nilpotent derivations on BB is denoted by LND⁡(B)\LND(B).

Let us recall an algebraic description of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions on affine varieties. Consider an affine variety XX. If α:𝔾a×X→X\alpha\colon\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}\times X\to X is a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on XX, then the composition

is a locally nilpotent derivation LND⁡(α)∈LND⁡(𝕂⁡[X])\LND(\alpha)\in\LND(\mathbb{K}[X]). Conversely, if ∂:𝕂⁡[X]→𝕂⁡[X]\partial\colon\mathbb{K}[X]\to\mathbb{K}[X] is a locally nilpotent derivation, then the map

exp(s∂)=∑n=0∞sn∂nn!:𝕂[X]→𝕂[X][s]\exp(s\partial)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{s^{n}\partial^{n}}{n!}\colon\mathbb{K}[X]\to\mathbb{K}[X][s]

defines an action A⁡(∂):𝔾a×X→X\A(\partial)\colon\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}\times X\to X. This correspondence between 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-actions on XX and locally nilpotent derivations on 𝕂⁡[X]\mathbb{K}[X] is bijective.

The following lemma is a simple technical observation that we will need later.

Lemma 2.1.

Consider a variety XX and a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action α\alpha on XX. Let U1,U2⊆XU_{1},U_{2}\subseteq X be two α\alpha-invariant affine open subsets and let f∈𝕂⁡(X)f\in\mathbb{K}(X) be a rational function on XX, regular on U1∪U2U_{1}\cup U_{2}. For each i=1,2i=1,2 denote ∂i=LND(α|Ui)∈LND(𝕂[Ui])\partial_{i}=\LND\left(\left.\kern-1.2pt{\alpha}\right|_{U_{i}}\right)\in\LND(\mathbb{K}[U_{i}]). Then ∂1(f)=∂2(f)\partial_{1}(f)=\partial_{2}(f) as rational functions on XX.

Proof.

where the horizontal arrows are restrictions of the action α\alpha and the vertical arrows are natural embeddings. Clearly, this diagram is commutative, hence the dual diagram

is also commutative. Therefore, we have ∂2(f)=∂1(f)|U2\partial_{2}(f)=\left.\kern-1.2pt{\partial_{1}(f)}\right|_{U_{2}} by construction.

Now consider the general case U1,U2⊆XU_{1},U_{2}\subseteq X and denote U3=U1∩U2U_{3}=U_{1}\cap U_{2}. Then U3⊆XU_{3}\subseteq X is an α\alpha-invariant affine open subset, so there exists a locally nilpotent derivation ∂3=LND(α|U3)∈\partial_{3}=\LND\left(\left.\kern-1.2pt{\alpha}\right|_{U_{3}}\right)\in ∈LND⁡(𝕂⁡[U3])\in\LND(\mathbb{K}[U_{3}]). By the first case we have

∂3(f)=∂1(f)|U3and∂3(f)=∂2(f)|U3,\partial_{3}(f)=\left.\kern-1.2pt{\partial_{1}(f)}\right|_{U_{3}}\quad\text{and}\quad\partial_{3}(f)=\left.\kern-1.2pt{\partial_{2}(f)}\right|_{U_{3}},

hence ∂1(f)=∂2(f)\partial_{1}(f)=\partial_{2}(f) in 𝕂⁡(X)\mathbb{K}(X). ∎

Definition 2.2.

Consider a variety XX. A cylinder in XX is an open subset UU together with an isomorphism U≅𝔸1×ZU\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z for some variety ZZ. By a fiber of a cylinder UU we mean a fiber of the projection U→ZU\to Z to the second factor. We call the projection U→𝔸1U\to\mathbb{A}^{1} to the first factor the level function of the cylinder UU.

Definition 2.3.

Let α:𝔾a×X→X\alpha\colon\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}\times X\to X be a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on a variety XX. We say that α\alpha is cylindrical if there is an isomorphism X≅𝔸1×ZX\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z for some variety ZZ such that α\alpha acts by translations along the first factor.

Let BB be a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra and ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\LND(B). An element b∈Bb\in B is called a slice of ∂\partial if ∂(b)=1\partial(b)=1. Assume that XX is an affine variety, B=𝕂⁡[X]B=\mathbb{K}[X] and α=A⁡(∂)\alpha=A(\partial) is the corresponding 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on XX. Then by Slice Theorem [3, Corollary 1.26] the action α\alpha is cylindrical if and only if the derivation ∂\partial admits a slice. Moreover, a function f∈𝕂⁡[X]f\in\mathbb{K}[X] is a slice of ∂\partial if and only if ff is a level function of a cylinder X≅𝔸1×ZX\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z and α\alpha is cylindrical with respect to this isomorphism.

The following result is a generalization of [11, Lemma 2.3] for arbitrary varieties.

Proposition 2.4.

Let XX be a variety and α\alpha be a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on XX. Assume that there is an isomorphism X≅𝔸1×ZX\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z such that every 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fiber is an orbit of α\alpha. Then α\alpha is cylindrical.

Proof.

Consider a covering Z=⋃i∈IUiZ=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_{i} of ZZ by open affine charts. For each i∈Ii\in I denote Vi=𝔸1×UiV_{i}=\mathbb{A}^{1}\times U_{i}. Then X=⋃i∈IViX=\bigcup_{i\in I}V_{i} is a covering of XX by affine α\alpha-invariant cylinders. For each i∈Ii\in I denote

∂i=LND(α|Vi)∈LND(𝕂[Vi]).\partial_{i}=\LND\left(\left.\kern-1.2pt{\alpha}\right|_{V_{i}}\right)\in\LND(\mathbb{K}[V_{i}]).

Denote by ss the level function of the cylinder X≅𝔸1×ZX\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z. By Lemma 2.1 the functions hi=∂i(s)∈𝕂⁡[Vi]⊆𝕂⁡(X)h_{i}=\partial_{i}(s)\in\mathbb{K}[V_{i}]\subseteq\mathbb{K}(X) can be glued together, defining a function h∈𝕂⁡[X]h\in\mathbb{K}[X]. By the argument from [11, Lemma 2.3], applied to each chart ViV_{i}, we have h∈𝕂⁡[Z]⊆𝕂⁡[X]h\in\mathbb{K}[Z]\subseteq\mathbb{K}[X], the function hh is invertible and

α⁡(s,(u,z))=(u+s​h,z)\alpha\big(s,(u,z)\big)=(u+sh,z)

for all s∈𝔾as\in\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}} and (u,z)∈𝔸1×Z(u,z)\in\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z. Conjugating the action α\alpha by the isomorphism

ϕ:𝔸1×Z→𝔸1×Z,ϕ⁡(u,z)=(uh,z),\phi\colon\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z\to\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z,\quad\phi(u,z)=\left(\frac{u}{h},z\right),

we obtain an action

s⋅(u,z)=ϕ⁡(α⁡(s,ϕ−1​(u,z)))=ϕ⁡(α⁡(s,(u​h,z)))=ϕ⁡(u​h+s​h,z)=(u+s,z).s\cdot(u,z)=\phi\Big(\alpha\big(s,\ \phi^{-1}(u,z)\big)\Big)=\phi\Big(\alpha\big(s,\ (uh,z)\big)\Big)=\phi(uh+sh,z)=(u+s,z).

Therefore, α\alpha is cylindrical. ∎

Let XX be an affine variety. By [6, Proposition 3.1.5] every 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on XX gives rise to a principal cylinder in XX. Namely, if α:𝔾a×X→X\alpha\colon\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}\times X\to X is a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on XX, then there exists an α\alpha-invariant principal cylinder U⊆XU\subseteq X such that α|U\left.\kern-1.2pt{\alpha}\right|_{U} is cylindrical.

Definition 2.5.

Let α:𝔾a×X→X\alpha\colon\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}\times X\to X be a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on a variety XX. By an α\alpha-cylinder we mean an α\alpha-invariant cylinder U⊆XU\subseteq X such that α|U\left.\kern-1.2pt{\alpha}\right|_{U} is cylindrical.

Let BB be a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra and ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\LND(B). The plinth ideal of the derivation ∂\partial is the set

pl⁡(∂)=Ker⁡(∂)∩Im⁡(∂).\pl(\partial)=\Ker(\partial)\cap\mIm(\partial).

This is an ideal in the algebra Ker⁡(∂)\Ker(\partial).

The following result is a description of the set of functions h∈𝕂⁡[X]h\in\mathbb{K}[X] that define a principal α\alpha-cylinder 𝔻X​(h)\mathbb{D}_{X}(h).

Theorem 2.6.

Let XX be an affine variety, α\alpha be a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on XX, and h∈𝕂⁡[X]h\in\mathbb{K}[X]. Denote ∂=LND⁡(α)∈LND⁡(𝕂⁡[X])\partial=\LND(\alpha)\in\LND(\mathbb{K}[X]). Then 𝔻X​(h)\mathbb{D}_{X}(h) is an α\alpha-cylinder if and only if hn∈pl⁡(∂)h^{n}\in\pl(\partial) for some n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

Proof.

Assume that there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that hn∈pl⁡(∂)h^{n}\in\pl(\partial). Since 𝔻X​(h)=𝔻X​(hn)\mathbb{D}_{X}(h)=\mathbb{D}_{X}(h^{n}), we may assume that h∈pl⁡(∂)h\in\pl(\partial). The assertion now follows from the construction in [6, Proposition 3.1.5].

Conversely, denote U=𝔻X​(h)U=\mathbb{D}_{X}(h) and assume that U≅𝔸1×ZU\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z is an α\alpha-cylinder. The LND ∂\partial extends to an LND on 𝕂⁡[U]⊇𝕂⁡[X]\mathbb{K}[U]\supseteq\mathbb{K}[X]. Then, since hh is an invertible element of the algebra 𝕂⁡[U]\mathbb{K}[U], we have ∂(h)=0\partial(h)=0. Moreover,

𝕂⁡[U]=𝕂​[X]h≅𝕂⁡[Z]​[s],\mathbb{K}[U]=\mathbb{K}[X]_{h}\cong\mathbb{K}[Z][s],

where 𝕂[Z]=Ker∂\mathbb{K}[Z]=\Ker\partial and ∂(s)=1\partial(s)=1. There exist f∈𝕂⁡[X]f\in\mathbb{K}[X] and n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that s=fhn.s=\frac{f}{h^{n}}. Therefore,

hn​s∈𝕂⁡[X]and∂(hn​s)=hn∈pl⁡(∂)h^{n}s\in\mathbb{K}[X]\quad\text{and}\quad\partial(h^{n}s)=h^{n}\in\pl(\partial)

as required. ∎

Corollary 2.7.

Let XX, α\alpha and ∂\partial be as in Theorem 2.6. Let {Ui}i∈I\{U_{i}\}_{i\in I} be the set of all principal α\alpha-cylinders in XX. Then

X∖⋃i∈IUi=𝕍X​(pl⁡(∂)).X\setminus\bigcup_{i\in I}U_{i}=\mathbb{V}_{X}\big(\pl(\partial)\big).

It is worth to mention here the equality 𝕍X(Im∂)=Fix(α)\mathbb{V}_{X}(\mIm\partial)=\Fix(\alpha).

Corollary 2.8.

Let XX, α\alpha and ∂\partial be as in Theorem 2.6. Assume that pl⁡(∂)⊆Ker⁡(∂)\pl(\partial)\subseteq\Ker(\partial) is a principal ideal. Then there exists a maximal principal α\alpha-cylinder in XX.

Note that by a result of Bonnet, Daigle, and Kaliman [2, Theorem 1.5] if X=𝔸3X=\mathbb{A}^{3}, then pl⁡(∂)\pl(\partial) is a principal ideal in Ker⁡(∂)\Ker(\partial).

3. Examples

The first example is a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action α\alpha on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} such that 𝔸3∖Fix⁡(α)\mathbb{A}^{3}\setminus\Fix(\alpha) is not an α\alpha-cylinder. Note that there is no such action on 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}. Indeed, by a result of Rentschler [10] every 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} is conjugate to an action of the form s⋅(x,y)=(x+s​p,y)s\cdot(x,y)=(x+sp,y) for some p∈𝕂⁡[y]p\in\mathbb{K}[y]. Then Fix⁡(α)=𝕍𝔸2​(p)\Fix(\alpha)=\mathbb{V}_{\mathbb{A}^{2}}(p) and 𝔸2∖Fix⁡(α)\mathbb{A}^{2}\setminus\Fix(\alpha) is a cylinder 𝔸1×𝔻𝔸1​(f)\mathbb{A}^{1}\times\mathbb{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}(f).

Example 3.1.

Consider an LND

∂=y​∂∂x+z​∂∂y∈LND⁡(𝕂⁡[x,y,z]).\partial=y\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+z\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\in\LND(\mathbb{K}[x,y,z]).

The corresponding 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action α\alpha on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} is

s⋅(x,y,z)=(x+s​y+12​s2​z,y+s​z,z).s\cdot(x,y,z)=\left(x+sy+\frac{1}{2}s^{2}z,\ y+sz,\ z\right).

Denote 𝕂×=𝕂∖{0}\mathbb{K}^{\times}=\mathbb{K}\setminus\{0\}. The orbits of α\alpha are parabolas

z=λ,x=12​λ​y2+az=\lambda,\quad x=\frac{1}{2\lambda}y^{2}+a

for some λ∈𝕂×\lambda\in\mathbb{K}^{\times} and a∈𝕂a\in\mathbb{K}; lines

z=0,y=λz=0,\quad y=\lambda

for some λ∈𝕂×\lambda\in\mathbb{K}^{\times}; and fixed points

z=0,y=0,x=az=0,\quad y=0,\quad x=a

for some a∈𝕂a\in\mathbb{K}. One can check that

Ker⁡(∂)=𝕂⁡[z,y2−2​x​z]andpl⁡(∂)=Ker⁡(∂)⋅z.\Ker(\partial)=\mathbb{K}[z,\ y^{2}-2xz]\quad\text{and}\quad\pl(\partial)=\Ker(\partial)\cdot z.

Although U=𝔸3∖Fix⁡(α)U=\mathbb{A}^{3}\setminus\Fix(\alpha) is a cylinder U≅𝔸1×(𝔸2∖{(0,0)})U\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times\big(\mathbb{A}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}\big), we claim that UU is not an α\alpha-cylinder. Assume the contrary that there is an isomorphism ϕ:U→𝔸1×Z\phi\colon U\to\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z such that α|U\left.\kern-1.2pt{\alpha}\right|_{U} is cylindrical with respect to ϕ\phi. Denote by ff the level function of ϕ\phi. Since Fix⁡(α)\Fix(\alpha) has codimension greater than one in 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}, we have f∈𝕂⁡[𝔸3]f\in\mathbb{K}[\mathbb{A}^{3}]. Consider an α\alpha-invariant subset V=𝔻𝔸3​(z)V=\mathbb{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{3}}(z). The isomorphism ϕ\phi restricts to an isomorphism ϕ|V:V→𝔸1×Z′\left.\kern-1.2pt{\phi}\right|_{V}\colon V\to\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z^{\prime} with a level function f|V\left.\kern-1.2pt{f}\right|_{V}. Therefore, f|V\left.\kern-1.2pt{f}\right|_{V} is a slice of ∂\partial on 𝕂⁡[V]=𝕂⁡[x,y,z,z−1]\mathbb{K}[V]=\mathbb{K}[x,y,z,z^{-1}]. It is easy to see that every such slice has the form

yz+h⁡(z,z−1,y2−2​x​z)\frac{y}{z}+h(z,\ z^{-1},\ y^{2}-2xz)

for some polynomial hh, but these functions are not regular on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}, which is a contradiction.

The second example is a free 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action α\alpha on an affine surface XX such that XX cannot be covered by α\alpha-cylinders. Again, there is no such action on 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}. We will need the following description of cylinders in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}.

Lemma 3.2.

Let U⊆ℙ2U\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{2} be a cylinder U≅𝔸1×CU\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times C. Then UU is affine and CC is isomorphic to an open subset of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}.

Proof.

Clearly, CC is a smooth curve. We claim that CC is rational. Indeed, the open embedding U⊆ℙ2U\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{2} induces a surjection of divisor class groups Cl⁡(ℙ2)→Cl⁡(U)\Cl(\mathbb{P}^{2})\to\Cl(U). Since Cl⁡(ℙ2)≅ℤ\Cl(\mathbb{P}^{2})\cong\mathbb{Z} and Cl⁡(U)≅Cl⁡(C)\Cl(U)\cong\Cl(C), we see that Cl⁡(C)\Cl(C) is a quotient group of ℤ\mathbb{Z}. In particular, Cl⁡(C^)\Cl(\hat{C}) is a finitely generated group, where C^\hat{C} is a smooth projective model of CC. It follows that the genus of C^\hat{C} is zero, hence CC is rational.

A smooth rational curve is isomorphic to an open subset of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, so it suffices to show that C≠ℙ1C\neq\mathbb{P}^{1}. But if C=ℙ1C=\mathbb{P}^{1}, then the curves {0}×ℙ1\{0\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} and {1}×ℙ1\{1\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} in UU are disjoint and closed in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}, which is a contradiction. ∎

Example 3.3.

Consider a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action α\alpha on ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} defined by the formula

s⋅(x:y:z)=(x+sy+12s2z:y+sz:z).s\cdot(x:y:z)=\left(x+sy+\frac{1}{2}s^{2}z\ :\ y+sz\ :\ z\right).

One can obtain this action from the action in Example 3.1 by passing to the quotient of 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} by the standard action of scalar matrices. The only fixed point of α\alpha is (1:0:0)(1:0:0) and the closures of other orbits of α\alpha are quadrics

x​z=y22+a​z2xz=\frac{y^{2}}{2}+az^{2}

for a∈𝕂a\in\mathbb{K} and the line z=0z=0. The affine variety

X=ℙ2∖{y2=2xz}X=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\{y^{2}=2xz\}

is α\alpha-invariant and the induced action α|X\left.\kern-1.2pt{\alpha}\right|_{X} has no fixed points.

Denote h=y2−2​x​zh=y^{2}-2xz. The algebra of regular functions on XX is the subalgebra in 𝕂⁡(x,y,z)\mathbb{K}(x,y,z) of functions of the form f/hnf/h^{n}, where nn is a non-negative integer and f∈𝕂⁡[x,y,z]f\in\mathbb{K}[x,y,z] is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 2​n2n. One check that

Ker⁡(∂)=𝕂⁡[z2/h]andpl⁡(∂)=Ker⁡(∂)⋅z2h.\Ker(\partial)=\mathbb{K}[z^{2}/h]\quad\text{and}\quad\pl(\partial)=\Ker(\partial)\cdot\frac{z^{2}}{h}.

Let us show that every cylinder U⊆XU\subseteq X is a principal proper subset. First, XX is not cylinder, since by Lemma 3.2 we have Cl⁡(U)=0\Cl(U)=0 but Cl⁡(X)≅ℤ/2​ℤ\Cl(X)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}. Therefore, U⊊XU\subsetneq X is a proper subset. The variety XX is smooth and the cylinder UU is affine by Lemma 3.2, so the complement X∖UX\setminus U is of pure codimension one. Since Cl⁡(X)≅ℤ/2​ℤ\Cl(X)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} we conclude that UU is principal. Thus, from Corollary 2.7 we deduce that the union of all α\alpha-cylinders in XX is the proper subset z≠0z\neq 0.

In the third example we show that for affine XX there may be an affine α\alpha-cylinder U⊆XU\subseteq X which cannot be covered by principal α\alpha-cylinders.

Example 3.4.

Consider a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} defined by an LND y​∂∂x+z​∂∂yy\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+z\frac{\partial}{\partial y} as in Example 3.1. The Danielewski surface

X={y2−2xz−1=0}X=\{y^{2}-2xz-1=0\}

is invariant with respect to this action. Denote by α\alpha the restriction of this action to XX and let ∂=LND⁡(α)∈LND⁡(𝕂⁡[X])\partial=\LND(\alpha)\in\LND(\mathbb{K}[X]). Let U⊆XU\subseteq X be the complement to the orbit z=y−1=0z=y-1=0. The extension of ∂\partial to 𝕂⁡[U]\mathbb{K}[U] admits a slice y+1z=2​xy−1\frac{y+1}{z}=\frac{2x}{y-1}, hence UU is an α\alpha-cylinder

U≅𝔸1×𝔸1(x,y,z)↦(z,y+1z)((u​v−2)​v2,u​v−1,u)↤(u,v).\begin{array}[]{rcl}U&\cong&\mathbb{A}^{1}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\\ (x,y,z)&\mapsto&\left(z,\frac{y+1}{z}\right)\\ \left(\frac{(uv-2)v}{2},\ uv-1,\ u\right)&\mapsfrom&(u,v)\end{array}.

On the other hand, we see that

Ker⁡(∂)=𝕂⁡[z]andpl⁡(∂)=Ker⁡(∂)⋅z.\Ker(\partial)=\mathbb{K}[z]\quad\text{and}\quad\pl(\partial)=\Ker(\partial)\cdot z.

By Corollary 2.7 the union of all principal α\alpha-cylinders in XX is equal to

𝔻X(z)=U∖{z=y+1=0}.\mathbb{D}_{X}(z)=U\setminus\{z=y+1=0\}.

Therefore, UU cannot be covered by principal α\alpha-cylinders.

The final example is a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action α\alpha on 𝔸4\mathbb{A}^{4} such that 𝔻𝔸4​(pl⁡(∂))\mathbb{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{4}}\big(\pl(\partial)\big) is not an α\alpha-cylinder. By Corollaries 2.7 and 2.8 we would need the plinth ideal pl⁡(∂)\pl(\partial) to be non-principal, hence no such actions occur for 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}.

Example 3.5.

Consider an LND

∂=u​∂∂x+v​∂∂y∈LND⁡(𝕂⁡[x,y,u,v]).\partial=u\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\in\LND(\mathbb{K}[x,y,u,v]).

The corresponding 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{a}}-action α\alpha on 𝔸4\mathbb{A}^{4} is

s⋅(x,y,u,v)=(x+s​u,y+s​v,u,v).s\cdot(x,y,u,v)=(x+su,\ y+sv,\ u,\ v).

One can check that

Ker⁡(∂)=𝕂⁡[u,v,x​v−y​u]andpl⁡(∂)=Ker⁡(∂)⋅u+Ker⁡(∂)⋅v.\Ker(\partial)=\mathbb{K}[u,\ v,\ xv-yu]\quad\text{and}\quad\pl(\partial)=\Ker(\partial)\cdot u+\Ker(\partial)\cdot v.

Using an argument similar to the one from Example 3.1, we can show that the cylinder U=U= =𝔻𝔸4​(pl⁡(∂))≅𝔸2×(𝔸2∖{(0,0)})=\mathbb{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{4}}\big(\pl(\partial)\big)\cong\mathbb{A}^{2}\times\big(\mathbb{A}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}\big) is not an α\alpha-cylinder. Denote V=𝔻𝔸4​(u)V=\mathbb{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{4}}(u). An isomorphism U≅𝔸1×ZU\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Z making UU an α\alpha-cylinder would define a level function, which is regular on 𝔸4\mathbb{A}^{4} since the codimension of 𝔸4∖U\mathbb{A}^{4}\setminus U is greater than one. This level function restricts to a slice of ∂\partial on 𝕂⁡[V]=𝕂⁡[x,y,u,u−1,v]\mathbb{K}[V]=\mathbb{K}[x,y,u,u^{-1},v]. Every such slice has the form

xu+h⁡(u,u−1,v,x​v−y​u)\frac{x}{u}+h(u,\ u^{-1},\ v,\ xv-yu)

for some polynomial hh. This is a contradiction with regularity of the level function.
